name: Orbital contouring surgery

card.summary: Orbital contouring surgery reshapes or rebuilds the bony eye socket and rim, which in appearance terms changes how deep-set, hooded or asymmetric the eyes look and how the brow and upper cheek frame them.
card.note: Major facial bone surgery near the eye; the research base is mainly trauma reconstruction, with cosmetic use described mostly by individual surgeons.

quick.overview:
The orbit is the bony socket that holds the eye. Orbital contouring surgery changes its shape: reducing a prominent brow or rim so eyes look less hidden, building up a deficient area, or correcting a socket that is asymmetric or enlarged after injury. In looksmaxxing talk it falls under hardmaxxing, the group of surgical changes to facial structure, and is tied to ideas such as "hunter eyes" and eye-area support.

Most published research comes from orbital fracture repair, where surgeons rebuild the socket with titanium mesh, polyethylene, resorbable sheets or the patient's own bone, increasingly with computer planning and navigation. Cosmetic reshaping in healthy people is described by individual surgeons rather than by large trials.
quick.how: Reconstruction surgery uses CT scans to plan, then places a preformed or patient-specific implant or graft to restore the socket's shape, sometimes with intraoperative navigation to match the other side. Cosmetic rim or brow reshaping in the surgeons' accounts is reached through incisions such as a scalp (coronal) incision. Recovery involves swelling, and follow-up measures eye position and movement.
quick.risks: Reported complications of orbital surgery include diplopia, eye-position change (enophthalmos or the reverse), eyelid and tear-duct problems, infection, implant issues and numbness; surgeons also stress that the eye's position is limited by the optic nerve and that vision risk is part of every orbital procedure. A scalp incision, described by one surgeon as a bigger trade-off for men, leaves a scar. Choice of a qualified facial plastic, craniofacial or oculoplastic surgeon is the standard guidance.

lead: Orbital contouring surgery is an umbrella label for procedures that alter the bony orbit, the socket that surrounds the eye, and the rim that frames it. In the medical literature the work is usually called orbital reconstruction and is performed to repair fractures, correct posttraumatic deformity, or rebuild after tumor surgery. In looksmaxxing and cosmetic contexts the same toolkit is described for cosmetic reshaping: reducing a heavy rim or brow so the eyes look less deep-set, or augmenting a flat rim.[1][2][8]

Surgeons writing about cosmetic use say prominent orbital rims form much of the bony box around the eye, and that when the outer bone is prominent the eye can look deep-set or hidden. Dr. Barry Eppley states the upper and outer rim can be reshaped but that access generally means a scalp incision, a more significant concern for men than for many women.[9]

The bulk of the research is reconstructive: reviews on anatomic versus volumetric reconstruction, computer-guided planning, patient-specific implants and implant materials, plus trials comparing titanium mesh with cranial bone graft.[1][2][5][6]

chain: Bone around the socket is reshaped, reduced or rebuilt
Eye position, brow and rim shape change
Eyes appear less hidden or more symmetrical
angle.text: The orbit's bony shape determines much of how deep-set or open the eye looks. Surgery changes that shape directly, whether rebuilding after injury or, per surgeons' cosmetic accounts, reducing a prominent rim or brow.

infobox: Titanium mesh, porous polyethylene, resorbable sheets, cranial bone graft [4][5][6]

paras: The orbit is a bony cavity of several bones that protects the eye and holds its muscles. Surgery on it falls into reconstruction (restoring volume and shape after fracture or resection) and contouring (reducing or adding bone at the rim, brow or lateral wall). Reviews of reconstruction stress that restoring the anatomic shape, rather than just filling volume, improves outcomes, and that endoscopic views and mirror-image overlay from the uninjured side help fine-tune implants.[1]

Cosmetic rim work is described mainly by individual surgeons. Dr. Eppley's pages say the rim around the eye can be reshaped, particularly the upper part under the brow and the outer side, and frame the decision as whether the scalp incision is a worthwhile trade-off.[9]

Reconstruction implants have included cranial bone grafts, titanium mesh, porous polyethylene and polydioxanone sheets.[4][5][6][7] A comparison of 58 pure blowout fractures assessed adequacy of reconstruction with cranial bone grafts versus titanium mesh on CT scans.[6]

Computer-assisted planning has been a major development. A 2002 study investigated navigation with virtual reconstruction to achieve orbital symmetry,[3] a 2015 review described planning software, navigation, patient-specific implants and intra-operative imaging,[2] and a prospective multicenter study compared standard preformed with individualized implants for precision.[11]

Orbital reviews note that eye injuries can threaten sight and that facial wounds can damage tear ducts and nerves.[12] Reconstruction research tracks eye position (exophthalmometry) before, during and after surgery because positional errors affect appearance.[1] A trial of 120 blow-out fracture patients examined postoperative eye-movement training in recovery.[13]

Within hardmaxxing discussions, orbital work sits with other eye-area structural ideas, such as support of the infraorbital rim and the brow ridge, and is typically described as a surgical rather than a home route. News coverage of the movement lists maxillofacial surgery as frequently proposed and discussed among its participants.[15]

Human studies are on orbital reconstruction for trauma. A comparative study of 58 patients examined cranial bone graft versus titanium mesh;[6] a prospective multicenter study compared preformed with individualized implants;[11] a 49-patient trial of titanium mesh with and without navigation for posttraumatic enophthalmos was reported in a Chinese stomatology journal;[16] a 120-patient randomized trial studied oculomotor training after reconstruction.[13] No controlled trial has studied orbital contouring for cosmetic purposes in healthy people.
